kanbanCards.html: BUG (operator + lead-observed 2026-06-12). Copilot CLI reported "Denied by preToolUse hook (hook errored)" on the LEAD's tool calls (a member spawn + a listener re-arm) -- an actual hook EXECUTION failure -> tool denied (fail-closed), NOT a normal block. LEAD DIAGNOSIS (read-only): hook LOGIC is fine (run directly: clean {decision:block} when review-required, empty/exit-0 when allowed, 187-301ms). Failures were TRANSIENT, at the moment of spawning a 4th member WHILE 3 freshly-spawned members were doing SessionStart + arming listeners (spawn-burst spike; ~36 live node procs). crews fires a fresh node subprocess PER hook fire; under that process-table/CPU saturation an individual hook invocation can fail to spawn/complete within the Copilot CLI hook window -> "hook errored" -> fail-closed. Self-heals after the burst. locator-failures.jsonl shows a storm of concurrent role-guard hook fires from the new member sessions (019ebefc-*) at that timestamp. DISTINCT FACET from crews-hook-timeout-under-lock-contention (merged) / crews-codex-12s-hook-timeout-ceiling (archived): trigger is PROCESS-SPAWN SATURATION during a concurrent SessionStart burst, not just manifest-lock timeout. Mitigation candidates: hook self-retry/backoff on transient spawn failure; lighter hook fast-path under contention; throttle SessionStart hook work; OR operating guidance to stagger lead spawns. NON-BLOCKING (retry works) but a real reliability facet at higher member concurrency.

INVESTIGATION DONE (2026-06-12, read-only member investigate-hook-errored; findings @ .ralph/investigations/crews-pretooluse-hook-errored-under-concurrent-spawn-burst/findings.md). VERDICT: broad hypothesis CONFIRMED, narrow one refuted. Best explained as a RUNTIME-level Copilot hook child missing its 30s response window during a fresh-node SessionStart/arming BURST -- NOT a pre-tool-use.js logic exception, and DISTINCT from the older deterministic 5s lock-budget bug. EVIDENCE: Copilot registers preToolUse as a fresh node hooks/copilot-pre-tool-use.js subprocess with timeoutSec: 30; the wrapper emits valid JSON even on handled failures; SessionStart/arm paths fan out synchronous manifest/lock/filesystem work across many sibling Node procs -> a saturation spike starves an individual hook child. TOP MITIGATION: STAGGER/THROTTLE concurrent spawns first (operating discipline -- already being applied by the lead). CODE follow-ups: trim SessionStart critical-path work, then add a cheaper already-armed-lead PreToolUse fast path. READY FOR PLAN (code-side mitigations).

kanbanCards.html: FOLLOW-UP (filed 2026-06-14 from investigate-bracketed-paste-win; findings @ .ralph/investigations/codex-bracketed-paste-fails-windows-terminal/findings.md). LONG-TERM "better thing" for paste on Windows: make TRUE bracketed paste work in Windows Terminal so codex receives one Event::Paste(String) instead of a key-event flood. ROOT CAUSE (source-verified): on Windows codex reads crossterm 0.28.1 (git 87db8bf) WinAPI INPUT_RECORD events and CLEARS ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT (tui/src/tui.rs:1263-1275); crossterm's bracketed-paste parser is Unix-VT-only (unix/parse.rs:863-872), so the Windows source NEVER emits Event::Paste. CHANGE SURFACE (medium-to-high conflict): (1) stop clearing ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_INPUT for a VT-capable Windows input path (or a deliberate mode that enables it) -- but FIRST understand WHY the keep-VT-input-cleared sandbox patch (tui/src/tui.rs:255-305) exists; (2) use a VT-byte event reader that parses CSI 200~/201~ into one paste payload; (3) integrate with codex's Windows event thread + console-mode reassertion + keyboard-enhancement/alt-screen; (4) PREFER upstream-native crossterm support (or a crossterm bump with a Windows VT-input paste path) so the codex surface stays small. This is the proper fix that would also make option (A) (rely on bracketed paste, drop the heuristic) viable on Windows. SEPARATE from codex-paste-guard-perf-and-dropped-text (that one keeps the heuristic enabled + improves it as the near-term fix). BRAINSTORM-first (cross-cutting terminal-mode invariants). CODEX submodule.

kanbanCards.html: FEASIBILITY (operator 2026-06-12). Can a codex WORKFLOWS product (see codex-workflows-product-mvp) REPLACE the ralph-orchestration plugin, AND make its phases USER-EXTENSIBLE (third parties add/reorder phases by editing workflow data, not forking the plugin)? CRUX (operator refinement): ralph is DEEPLY NESTED/RECURSIVE -- it is not a flat brainstorm->plan->impl pipeline. Each phase is itself a multi-phase sub-workflow: e.g. IMPL = PRD generation -> review -> implementation -> DSAT gathering -> Phase-5a/5b convergence loops, and each sub-phase spawns its own sub-agents. So the make-or-break question is whether the codex workflow runtime supports NESTED/RECURSIVE sub-workflows + convergence loops + operator-interaction points, WITHIN the documented Claude-parity limits (16 concurrent agents, 1000 total/run, NO mid-run user input, NO direct FS/shell from the script). READ-ONLY analysis; feeds the MVP design (#1). Brainstorm/investigation member.

FEASIBILITY DONE (2026-06-12, read-only member investigate-ralph-as-workflow; findings @ .ralph/investigations/codex-workflows-replace-ralph-orchestration-feasibility/findings.md). VERDICT: PARTIAL-REPLACE. A codex workflows product can cover Ralph's root-owned autonomous slices, but NOT the full Ralph system or user-extensible Ralph-class phases yet. TOP BLOCKERS: (1) NO true nested workflow recursion -- spawn_agent is effectively root-only with default DEPTH 1 (matches the known fork subagent-depth gate); Ralph's impl = PRD-gen -> review -> impl -> DSAT -> 5a/5b each spawning sub-agents needs >1 depth. (2) NO persisted workflow-run registry / resume model comparable to Ralph's job-state.json + artifact state. (3) Ralph's data-dependent convergence loops need first-class LOOP/BRANCH semantics, not a flat phase list. RECOMMENDATION: use Ralph as the CANONICAL complex benchmark for the workflows MVP, but scope MVP parity to SHALLOW / root-owned workflows FIRST. Directly grounds codex-workflows-product-mvp requirements (nesting depth, run-registry/resume, loop/branch).

THE CRUX -- NESTING/RECURSION: ralph is NOT a flat pipeline. It is deeply nested. Map ralph's actual structure from source: the ralph plugin lives at ai-developer-toolkit/plugins/ralph/ (skills, scripts, src). Document the real phase tree -- e.g. top-level brainstorm -> plan -> impl, where IMPL itself = convert-to-ralph-PRD -> per-story implementation loop -> Phase 5a code review-fix convergence (multi-round) -> Phase 5b docs review-fix convergence -> DSAT/retrospective gathering -> followup-task gathering, and where individual steps spawn SUBAGENTS (e.g. the write/review children, the codex spawn_agent fan-out). THEN assess against the codex workflow runtime model (from the parity findings + codex multi-agent source core/src/tools/handlers/multi_agents_v2/ + features/src/feature_configs.rs + spec_plan.rs): 
1. NESTED SUB-WORKFLOWS: can a codex workflow phase itself BE a workflow (recursion)? Does the runtime/agent model allow a spawned agent to itself spawn a nested workflow run, and to what DEPTH? (Cross-reference any depth limits -- e.g. the fork subagent gate at tool_config.rs and the depth-limited-to-1 finding if it still applies.)
2. AGENT BUDGET: ralph fans out many agents across nested phases. Do Claude-parity limits (16 concurrent / 1000 total per run) + codex MultiAgentV2 max_concurrent_threads_per_session (default 4) accommodate ralph's real fan-out, or is per-phase budgeting needed?
3. CONVERGENCE LOOPS: Phase 5a/5b are iterate-until-clean loops (data-dependent iteration count). Can a workflow express a loop whose iteration count is decided at runtime by a reviewer verdict?
4. OPERATOR INTERACTION: ralph + the bookkeeper relay operator decisions (kind=question). The Claude workflow runtime documents NO mid-run user input. Is that a blocker for ralph's question-relay + approval pauses?
5. STATE/RESUME: ralph persists job-state.json + iteration manifests + worktrees. Can workflow run-state model that, and resume mid-job?
6. CROSS-ENGINE + CREWS: ralph today runs cross-engine (Claude/Copilot/codex) and is driven via the crews member model. A codex-native workflow runtime is codex-only -- what is lost (the non-codex engines, the cross-session crew model)?
7. USER-EXTENSIBILITY: if ralph phases were DEFINED as workflow data (declarative phase graph), could a third party add/reorder a phase without forking? What would the phase-definition format need (inputs/outputs, sub-agent recipes, convergence predicates)?

VERDICT: FULL-REPLACE / PARTIAL-REPLACE (which parts) / NOT-FEASIBLE, with the specific blockers, and a recommendation on whether the codex-workflows-product-mvp design should TARGET ralph as its canonical complex use case (driving nesting + loop + budget requirements into the MVP). Note conflict surface (fork-minimize).

prompts.brainstorm:
/brainstorm-with-ralph "How do we make the codex submodule's Rust workspace compile cleanly on this Windows dev box (and on any contributor's machine) so impl members can verify before push, instead of deferring to CI on tag-push?

## Why this matters

Today's reality (per auto-memory feedback_codex_fork_no_local_cargo):
- Local cargo is unavailable on this Windows machine.
- The publish path (codex/.claude/commands/publish-sandbox-patch.md) installs xwin + LLVM + V8 lib + other heavy deps ON-DEMAND for release cuts.
- Daily impl iteration pushes to gim-home/codex and lets .github/workflows/invariant-check.yml verify.

This is a real safety gap. The impl-codex-sandbox-setup-release member (just shipped) made 8 file changes to codex including publish-npm.yml and got Phase 5a code-review consensus 'looks fine' — but no compile happened. If the cargo build line in the workflow has a typo or the bin name is slightly off, the failure surfaces only when a release tag triggers CI, possibly days later, with no clear assignment to the impl session that introduced it.

We want: impl members can run `cargo check` or `cargo build --release` locally as part of Phase 5a, catch compile errors before pushing, and only fall back to CI for the end-to-end packaging verification.

## What we have today

- Windows 11 Enterprise dev box.
- Rust toolchain status: unknown — the brainstorm MUST verify (run `rustup show` and check what's installed).
- codex submodule Cargo workspace: monorepo with ~30+ crates including codex (main bin), codex-core, codex-windows-sandbox-rs, codex-command-runner, and various sandbox/auth/plugin crates.
- Known heavy dependencies (from publish-sandbox-patch.md): xwin (cross-compile shim for MSVC headers), LLVM (clang for some bindgen consumers), V8 lib (for the boa-engine or rusty_v8 JS interpreter inside codex's plugin/expression layer).
- Existing build infrastructure: .github/workflows/publish-npm.yml does the full Windows release build on `windows-latest` runners.
- CI invariant: .github/workflows/invariant-check.yml runs on push.

## Investigation step (mandatory before recommending)

Before any solution evaluation, the brainstorm member must:

1. **Reproduce the failure.** Run `cd D:/harness-efforts/codexu/codex && cargo build --release --bin codex 2>&1 | tee /tmp/codex-build-attempt.log`. Capture the FIRST error (subsequent errors often cascade from the first).
2. **Categorize the failure** by error class:
   - Missing native lib (linker error)?
   - Missing system header (compile error in -sys crate)?
   - Missing Rust toolchain feature (e.g., wasm32 target, MSVC target)?
   - Missing tool (clang, llvm-config, lld)?
   - Cargo registry/network issue (unlikely but check)?
3. **Identify the failing crate(s).** Read the error context to determine which crate triggered the failure. Trace back through Cargo.toml to see which feature flag or platform-specific dep introduced it.
4. **Check what publish-sandbox-patch.md installs.** That command is the canonical 'install everything needed for a release build.' Whatever it installs is by definition the answer to 'what's missing locally.' Reading that command's contents tells us 80% of the dependency map.

## Approaches to lens against (after step 1)

### A — Run publish-sandbox-patch's install steps once, then iterate normally

If publish-sandbox-patch.md already enumerates the install (xwin + LLVM + V8 + ...), run those steps ONCE on the dev machine. Subsequent cargo builds reuse the installed toolchain. Document the one-time install as a new contributor-setup script.

Pros: zero code change; minimum effort; matches the established release path.
Cons: heavy install (~5-10 GB for V8 lib alone); slow first build; may pollute the machine; multi-machine setup recurs.

### B — WSL2 dev environment

Move codex builds into WSL2 (Ubuntu). The Linux toolchain is simpler — install rustc + clang + standard libs via apt; no xwin/MSVC weirdness. Build target stays x86_64-pc-windows-msvc via cross-compile, OR build native Linux for development and cross-compile only for release.

Pros: faster install; easier reproduce; WSL2 is well-supported on Windows 11.
Cons: file-system perf (WSL2 mounts Windows files slowly); requires WSL2 already installed; pushes contributors to a Linux mental model even though the prod target is Windows.

### C — Devcontainer / GitHub Codespaces

Define a .devcontainer/devcontainer.json in codex with all build deps. Open codex in a Codespace or local devcontainer. Build inside the container.

Pros: reproducible across machines; zero local install footprint; CI-like dev environment.
Cons: requires Docker; networking lag; volume mounts add another perf layer.

### D — Minimize the dependency surface

Audit codex's Cargo.toml + feature flags. Identify deps that are only needed for runtime (V8, snmalloc?) and gate them behind features. Default-build = lean (no V8 etc.); release-build = full features. impl members do default-build for compile-check; CI does release-build for end-to-end verification.

Pros: long-term value; faster CI; smaller release artifacts.
Cons: invasive surgery on codex codebase; needs upstream codex coordination if any features become non-default in our fork; risk of feature-cfg bugs.

### E — Prebuilt binary cache + cargo-binstall pattern

For heavy deps (V8 lib), cache the build artifact in S3/GitHub Releases. cargo-binstall fetches the prebuilt instead of building from source.

Pros: skip the heaviest 80% of build time; viable if V8 is the actual bottleneck.
Cons: requires binary-cache infrastructure; not idiomatic Rust; brittle for security-sensitive crates.

### F — Just-in-time install (current state, but documented)

Keep the current model (CI is truth), but invest in: (1) faster CI feedback loop (push-to-pr-status in minutes), (2) better impl-member tooling that detects 'this change touches Rust' and prompts the operator to run /publish-sandbox-patch's verify mode before merging, (3) a 'cargo check on push' GitHub Actions workflow that runs in <2 minutes.

Pros: matches established workflow; minimum investment.
Cons: doesn't actually solve the safety gap; just makes the gap less risky.

### G — Devil's-advocate: don't build locally at all; trust CI

Is the safety gap real? How often does an impl member's Rust change actually break the build vs pass review + CI cleanly? Maybe the cost of local-build infra exceeds the cost of the occasional CI revert.

Must be pressure-tested: count the number of Rust changes in the last N codex commits, count how many failed CI on first push, compute the actual-failure rate.

## Deliverable

At the end of brainstorm Phase 5 (finalize), produce a `selected-direction.md` in `.ralph/brainstorms/codex-local-build/` capturing:

- The actual reproduced build error (copy-paste from cargo output) — grounds the rest of the analysis.
- Which crates / features are the actual bottleneck.
- Recommended approach (one of A-G or hybrid).
- Concrete next steps (one-time setup commands, doc edits, CI workflow additions, feature-flag changes — whatever the chosen approach needs).
- Acceptance criteria for the eventual impl (e.g., 'after setup, cargo build --release --bin codex completes in <X minutes on a fresh checkout').
- Open questions for operator that the planner should ask.

Do NOT chain into /plan-with-ralph. The bookkeeper spawns a fresh plan-codex-local-build member from the selected-direction.md per phase discipline.

## Reference reading + commands to run

- `codex/.claude/commands/publish-sandbox-patch.md` — the canonical install path; READ FIRST.
- `codex/.github/workflows/publish-npm.yml` — the CI build; what does it run before cargo build?
- `codex/.github/workflows/invariant-check.yml` — the per-push CI; mirror this for local cargo check?
- `codex/Cargo.toml` (workspace) + per-crate Cargo.toml files — feature flags + heavy deps.
- `rustup show` to verify toolchain state.
- `cargo metadata --manifest-path codex/Cargo.toml --format-version 1 | jq '.packages[] | select(.dependencies[] | .source == null and .kind != \"dev\")'` — inspect non-registry dependencies.

Lenses to deploy: feasibility (codex — actually try to run the build commands), product-reality (copilot — 'how often does the safety gap actually bite?'), simplification (does the chosen approach add more setup complexity than the gap costs?), devil's-advocate (is this premature optimization vs accepting the CI-is-truth model?). Plus a Claude general-purpose lens running the actual build attempt + dependency audit to produce the dependency map with file:line citations."

prompts.brainstorm:
/brainstorm-with-ralph "Rename the 'overview' concept across the project. The word is too generic — it doesn't tell a new contributor what the system actually IS. Candidates include roadmap, board, tracker, pipeline, workspace, catalog, atlas, registry. This brainstorm picks the name AND scopes the rename.

## Why this matters

Walk a fresh contributor into the codebase and ask 'what is .ralph-overview/data.json?' — the word 'overview' could mean anything (executive summary doc, system architecture diagram, project status report). The actual system is more specific: a hand-curated task roadmap (operator-authored intent: planPrompts, kanban cards, scope, descriptions) FUSED with watcher-derived runtime pipeline state (RalphStage, crewSessions, storyCompletion). The current name buries that meaning.

Downstream cost of the bad name: every doc that introduces the system has to spend a sentence explaining 'when we say overview we mean...'. Every new agent prompt that needs to reference it has to disambiguate. Operator-facing language ('the overview', 'overview viewer', 'overview bookkeeper') reads as a placeholder, not a system name.

## Naming candidates to lens against

The brainstorm should pressure-test at least these and synthesize any others that emerge:

- **roadmap** — captures the planning aspect; downside: doesn't convey runtime/pipeline state (a roadmap is static); collides slightly with plans/codexu-roadmap.md which IS a static doc.
- **board** — kanban-y; matches the existing kanban surface in TaskCommand; downside: too narrow (board implies the kanban view is primary, but the task list is primary).
- **tracker** — generic but accurate; downside: bland; collides with 'issue tracker' associations.
- **pipeline** — captures the flow brainstorm→plan→impl→ship; COLLIDES with crew name 'ralph-pipeline' — would force a crew rename or accept dual meaning.
- **workspace** — captures the meta-aspect; downside: VS Code workspace collision; doesn't convey 'roadmap of tasks'.
- **catalog** — formal; captures the curated aspect; downside: implies read-only/reference.
- **atlas** — evocative; conveys 'map of work'; downside: opaque without context.
- **registry** — too database-y.
- **directory** — too filesystem-y.
- **scoreboard** — too gamified.

## Scope-of-rename axis (separate from name choice)

The brainstorm MUST address: rename EVERYTHING, or rename only some layers?

1. **Full rename:** every surface (files, packages, plugin, types, MCP tools, bookkeeper role name, npm scripts, all docs). Maximum cost; cleanest end-state.
2. **Surface-only rename:** rename user-facing names (file names, npm scripts, plugin display name, docs) but keep internal types (OverviewTask, OverviewData) for back-compat. Lower cost; the type names become 'historical' and confuse future readers — but maybe acceptable.
3. **Plugin-package keeps old name, new files use new name:** the `ralph-overview` plugin stays named that (npm dependency cost of renaming a published package); files inside use the new name. Mixed signal but pragmatic.
4. **Add new alias, deprecate old:** ship the new name as additive; old names work via aliases for 1 minor; drop old names in v+2. Most expensive (twice as much code touched) but minimizes consumer breakage.

4. **Single-coordinated PR.** This rebrand should ship as ONE PR per repo (codexu + ai-developer-toolkit) to avoid half-renamed state.
5. **Must land AFTER overview-data-dynamic-stages-schema + overview-data-ship-manifest + overview-data-context-scalability.** Otherwise the rebrand churns through merge conflicts with those in-flight schema changes. Sequence the 4 tasks in dependency order.

command.name: happy-app-minimal-conflict-reduction-inherit-upstream
command.descriptionHtml: Minimal-conflict rebase for happy-app: re-triage the app hard-conflict surface under an AGGRESSIVE-REDUCE lens (revert non-essential divergences to upstream to inherit features; overlay essential ones; accept only the irreducible sync core) so upstream features flow in via merge. kanbanCards.html: OPERATOR REFRAME (2026-07-08): the goal is MINIMAL-CONFLICT REBASE, not per-feature adoption. Upstream app features do not flow in today because the fork DIVERGED on the same files (merge conflict -> take-ours -> feature dropped). To have ALL upstream features, REDUCE the fork divergence so upstream files merge cleanly: (1) REVERT-to-upstream where the fork change is NON-essential (inherit the feature, lose a non-essential tweak); (2) OVERLAY to sources/fork/ where the fork change IS essential (keep fork behavior + inherit upstream file); (3) ACCEPT permanent conflict only for the irreducible sync.ts/storage.ts. Essential fork divergences to KEEP: single-user, no-central-server, no-E2E, e-ink perf, removed voice/multi-account/encryption planes. Everything else is a REVERT candidate. Supersedes the conservative keep-all A0 triage + the per-feature opt-in framing (happy-app-upstream-feature-opt-ins-cli-1.1.10). Brainstorm-first: produce the essential-vs-nonessential boundary + per-file REVERT/OVERLAY/ACCEPT disposition for the app hard-conflict surface + expected post-reduction conflict count, then execute in waves.

FRAMING CORRECTION (operator 2026-07-08): do NOT revert/drop any fork behavior. MOVE it. Disposition model = (1) MOVE/OVERLAY (default for every REDUCIBLE file): relocate the fork divergence — essential OR non-essential — into a fork-only sources/fork/ module + keep the upstream-canonical file near-upstream + thin seam (R8 pattern), so the canonical file merges cleanly (inherits upstream features) while ALL fork behavior is preserved in the overlay; (2) ALIGN-to-upstream ONLY for pure convergent-noise files with NO intentional fork behavior to keep (narrow; not 'reverting a feature'); (3) ACCEPT-CONFLICT only for the irreducible sync core (sync.ts/storage.ts). The axis is REDUCIBLE(->MOVE, preserve) vs IRREDUCIBLE(->ACCEPT); never drop an intentional fork change. new/index.tsx -> MOVE (fork-own e-ink behind overlay), not revert. Voice removal stays an intentional KEEP-DELETED.

Brainstorm shipped @ 6ca3a002e (MOVE model). Of 59 app hard-conflict files: ~31 MOVE to sources/fork/* overlays+seams (fork behavior preserved, canonical files near-upstream so they inherit upstream features on future merges), ~0 ALIGN, ~5-7 IRREDUCIBLE ACCEPT (sync.ts/storage.ts/reducer/apiSocket/ops core), 8 KEEP-DELETED guards, 3 merge=ours. ZERO fork behaviors dropped. HONESTY CAVEAT: MOVE removes resolution COST+frequency (whole-file re-derivation -> 1-line seam re-apply), not the conflict-marker count to zero (seams can re-collide); the ~5-7 ACCEPT are the permanent expensive floor (upstream sync plane is seam-less). Wave plan W0(lineage done)->W1 MOVE-list/const->W2 renderers->W3 session-tree+screens->W4 new/index.tsx(route flag)->W5 plane residuals+i18n->W6 accept core; every wave gates encryptionDeletion.spec + e-ink spot-check. new/index.tsx=MOVE; voice=KEEP-DELETED; removed planes=KEEP-DELETED. 10 operator-decision calls.
